electricity.grid_emission_factor_note: Default is CEA weighted-average including RES & captive (0.7117 kgCO₂e/kWh, FY 2024-25). Other CEA factors (operating margin, build margin, combined margin) exist in knowledge-base/emissions/grid_factors.json and can be selected once the Factory contract exposes a selector. Factors are never averaged.
electricity.cost_coverage_limitation: MVP electricity cost is energy-only (INR/kWh × annual kWh). Demand (kVA/kW) charges, fixed charges, electricity duty and surcharges are excluded because the Factory contract does not supply contracted_demand_kva or maximum_demand_kva. Treat annual_electricity_cost_inr (and therefore total_energy_cost_inr) as incomplete for any site that faces material demand charges. Full bill modelling requires the TariffEngine path with explicit demand inputs.

fuel.conversion_note: Daily CO₂ from emission_engine × operating_days_per_year → annual_fuel_co2_tonnes. Never treat a *_day field as annual.

emissions_boundary.note: Fuel CO₂ is calculated from the IPCC-style emission factor stored for the fuel. Biogenic fuels still produce physical combustion CO₂; the project's reported fossil/biogenic accounting boundary is applied downstream by the recommendation / emissions boundary layer, not by zeroing the physical factor here.

industry.description: Industry profile for Indian textile manufacturing covering spinning, weaving, knitting, wet processing, dyeing, printing, finishing and associated steam, thermal-fluid and electrical utility systems. Textile is not a single-temperature process: spinning and weaving are predominantly electricity-intensive, while wet processing, dyeing, printing, drying and finishing can require substantial thermal energy through steam, hot water, thermic-fluid systems and direct-fired equipment.

india_sector_context.source: NITI Aayog, Roadmap for Green Transition of MSMEs, January 2026
india_sector_context.warning: The sector-level SEC and energy mix are benchmarks for the Indian MSME textile sector and must not be treated as the measured performance of an individual textile factory.

spinning.description: Conversion of fibres into yarn through opening, cleaning, carding, drawing, roving and spinning.

weaving.description: Conversion of yarn into fabric using power looms or shuttleless weaving machines.

wet_processing.description: Processing of textile fibres, yarns or fabrics using water, chemicals, heat and mechanical operations.

dyeing.description: Application and fixation of dyes to textile fibres, yarns or fabrics using controlled temperature, liquor ratio, chemical concentration and processing time.

printing.description: Application of dyes, pigments or printing pastes to textile substrates followed by drying and fixation.

finishing.description: Final mechanical and thermal treatment used to achieve required dimensions, appearance, handle and functional characteristics.

electric_boiler.optimizer_rule: Recommend only after comparing annualized electricity cost against current boiler fuel cost and verifying electrical capacity.

advantages: High efficiency at suitable temperature lift
industrial_heat_pump.optimizer_rule: Do not recommend heat pumps for high-temperature direct-fired duties merely because the industry is textile.

best_fit: Low and medium temperature process heat

temperature_fit.medium_temperature: Suitable where collector technology can meet required process temperature

advantages: Particularly relevant where local agricultural residue is abundant
biomass_boiler.optimizer_rule: Do not assume biomass is carbon-free or universally available; verify sustainable local supply and measured fuel properties.

best_fit: Replacing coal/pet coke in direct-fired equipment
natural_gas_or_png_transition.benefit: Lower local air pollutants and potentially lower direct CO2 intensity than coal or pet coke.
natural_gas_or_png_transition.constraint: Natural gas remains a fossil fuel and should not automatically outrank electrification or sustainable biomass.

waste_heat_recovery.optimizer_rule: Prioritize recovery when waste heat temperature, flow rate, operating hours and heat sink are sufficient.

best_fit: Facilities with simultaneous electricity and steam demand

variable_frequency_drive.optimizer_rule: Highest value where motor load varies with production or process demand.

efficient_compressed_air.warning: Compressed air should not be treated as a heat source; its primary relevance is electrical efficiency and recoverable compressor waste heat.

suitable: Industrial Heat Pump where required temperature is achievable
High-temperature Heat Pump where technically available
120_to_180_c.warning: Heat-pump feasibility depends on the actual required supply temperature and temperature lift; do not assume generic heat-pump capability.

generic_heat_pump_for_high_temperature_p.reason: Generic heat pumps should not be recommended where the process temperature exceeds the verified supply-temperature capability of the selected heat-pump technology.

biomass_for_all_processes.reason: Biomass suitability depends on fuel quality, sustainable supply, combustion equipment, emissions and process requirements.

solar_thermal_for_24x7_uninterrupted_pro.reason: Solar thermal normally requires thermal storage or a backup heat source for continuous textile operations.

electric_boiler_without_grid_capacity.reason: Electrical capacity, transformer loading and demand charges must be checked before electrifying substantial steam loads.

industry_route_rule.rule: Identify the textile subsector before technology selection.

thermal_vs_electrical_rule.weaving: Prioritize electrical efficiency and compressed-air optimization.
thermal_vs_electrical_rule.wet_processing: Prioritize thermal efficiency, heat recovery and process control.
thermal_vs_electrical_rule.dyeing: Prioritize steam/hot-water efficiency, liquor-ratio reduction, heat recovery and temperature control.
thermal_vs_electrical_rule.printing: Prioritize drying, curing and heat-recovery efficiency.
thermal_vs_electrical_rule.finishing: Prioritize stenter/dryer efficiency and exhaust heat recovery.

recommend_if: Required process temperature is within verified heat-pump supply range
Waste heat or ambient source temperature is sufficient
Electricity price permits acceptable operating economics
do_not_recommend_if: Required temperature is beyond verified technology capability

recommend_if: Renewable electricity is available or planned
Hot-water or medium-temperature thermal demand is available
Roof or land area is available
Process has sufficient daytime thermal demand
Backup or thermal storage is available where necessary
Existing boiler can be adapted or biomass boiler is economically justified

process_control_rule.reason: Textile wet processing often depends on accurate temperature, time, liquor ratio and chemical control.

msme_specific_reference.reason: Indian textile MSMEs have heterogeneous process configurations and fuel mixes; cluster-level and sector-level data should be used as priors, while plant-specific measurements should override them.

primary_sources: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
rules: Do not use one temperature for the entire textile industry.
Do not assume every textile plant is steam-intensive.
Spinning and weaving should be treated primarily as electrical loads.
Dyeing and wet processing should be treated as thermal plus electrical loads.
Use process-specific temperature data when available.
Use measured plant SEC instead of sector SEC when available.
Do not assume biomass is available at every site.
Do not recommend heat pumps solely because the industry is textile.
Check required process temperature before selecting a heat-pump pathway.
Check transformer and demand capacity before recommending major electrification.
Use technology-specific savings as reference ranges rather than guaranteed savings.
Treat case-study temperatures and savings as case-specific unless explicitly identified as a sector benchmark.

grid_factors.description: CEA CO₂ Baseline Database factors for the Indian Grid. Selection of which factor to use is an explicit accounting decision, not a silent default.

grid.name: Indian Grid
grid.scope: National interconnected electricity grid (unified Indian Grid)

accounting_policy.rationale: For MSME industrial baseline and recommendation work the project uses the generation-weighted average that includes renewable energy and captive injection. This is the location-based factor most representative of the electricity actually delivered by the Indian Grid. Operating Margin / Build Margin / Combined Margin remain available for CDM-style or marginal analyses and must be selected explicitly.
notes: CEA publishes several factors for different purposes. Averaging them is forbidden.
State-specific or DISCOM-specific factors are not yet in the Factory contract; national factor is used until then.
Factor is expressed as kgCO2e/kWh (numerically identical to tCO2/MWh).

default_factor.uncertainty: National average; actual plant/DISCOM intensity may differ. Replace with measured or contractual factor when available.

weighted_average.basis: Weighted average emission rate (excluding full RES/captive adjustment in some presentations)

weighted_average_including_res_and_capti.basis: Weighted average grid emission rate including renewable energy and captive power injection into the grid
weighted_average_including_res_and_capti.notes: Primary default for this project. Closely matches CEA published weighted average ~0.710 tCO2/MWh for FY 2024-25.

build_margin.basis: Build margin (recent capacity additions, including RE)

source.organization: Central Electricity Authority (CEA), Ministry of Power, Government of India
source.document: CO2 Baseline Database for the Indian Power Sector

notes: CEA treats the interconnected Indian electricity system as the unified Indian Grid.
Values are reported by CEA in tCO2/MWh; numerically identical when expressed as kgCO2e/kWh.
Do not average conflicting factors; select one basis and record it.
